name: Spanish
note: Latin American Spanish: ustedes for every plural you, c and z as s

alphabet.e: a rasped h, as in loch: jugo
the same rasped h before e and i: gente
hard g before e and i, the u silent: guerra
s before e and i in Latin America: cinco
the same sound as b: vaca
a soft b, lips not quite closed: lobo
th, as in this, between vowels: nada

units.title: BASICS
units.subtitle: Greetings, the people around a name, and the numbers up to twelve

tips.b: Spanish has two singular words for the person addressed. Tú goes with friends, family and children; usted goes with strangers, older people and anyone owed formality. The verb ending changes with the choice.
Buenos días runs until midday, buenas tardes from midday until dark, and buenas noches from dark onward. All three are plural in Spanish.

phrases.e: Thank you very much, see you later

tips.b: A Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows which: el for masculine, la for feminine. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine. The gender is listed beside each noun in this course.
The verb ending already names the subject, so yo, tú and él are dropped unless the sentence needs contrast or emphasis.
Latin America uses ustedes for any group, formal or not. The form vosotros belongs to Spain and does not appear in this course.
A written question begins with ¿ and ends with ?. The opening mark shows where the question starts inside a longer sentence.
Y joins two things, o offers a choice, and pero contrasts them. Y becomes e before a word beginning with the i sound, and o becomes u before the o sound.
Muy modifies an adjective or an adverb and never changes shape. Mucho modifies a verb, or counts a noun and then agrees with it.
Uno counts on its own, but before a masculine noun it becomes un and before a feminine noun una. The other numbers keep one form.
Spanish states age with tener and años: a person has years. Ser is never used for age.

phrases.e: There are four of us at home

units.title: EVERYDAY
units.subtitle: Food, drink, colour, and the members of a household

tips.h: The article is part of the noun
tips.b: A noun is worth learning with its article, because the article is the only visible mark of gender on many words. El pan and la carne give no clue in their endings.
A noun ending in a vowel adds -s; a noun ending in a consonant adds -es. The article turns plural with it: el becomes los, la becomes las.
A feminine noun beginning with a stressed a takes el in the singular, to keep two a sounds apart. The adjective stays feminine, and the plural returns to las.
Beber names the act of drinking. Tomar covers the same ground in most of Latin America and is the more common choice in speech.

phrases.e: I want a glass of milk

tips.b: A Spanish adjective normally stands after the noun it describes, the reverse of English order.
An adjective ending in -o has four forms: rojo, roja, rojos, rojas. An adjective ending in -e or in a consonant changes only for number: verde, verdes, azul, azules.
The masculine plural names a mixed group: los hermanos is brothers, or brothers and sisters together. Los padres means the parents.
Mi, tu and su stand before the noun and agree only in number: mi hermano, mis hermanos. Su covers his, her, their and the possessive of usted.

units.title: ACTIONS
units.subtitle: The present tense, describing words, questions, and how to say no

tips.b: Every Spanish verb ends in -ar, -er or -ir. The ending is dropped and a personal ending is added in its place. For an -ar verb such as hablar the present tense runs -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an.
An -er verb takes -o, -es, -e, -emos, -en. An -ir verb matches it except in the nosotros form, which ends -imos. The ustedes and ellos form ends -en for both.
Ser states what something is: identity, origin, profession and lasting traits. Estar states how or where something is at the moment: location, health and mood.

phrases.e: We live in a big house

tips.b: An adjective takes the gender and number of the noun it describes: un libro nuevo, una casa nueva, unos libros nuevos, unas casas nuevas.
Bueno and malo drop the final -o before a masculine singular noun. Grande shortens to gran before any singular noun, and in that position it praises the noun instead of measuring it.
Qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo and cuánto take a written accent when they ask. The same words without the accent introduce a statement.
A question puts the verb before its subject, and no extra word stands in for the English do or does.
Two words with an accent ask the question; one word without an accent gives the reason.
A sentence is negated by placing no directly in front of the verb. Nothing else changes.
When nada, nadie, nunca or ninguno stand after the verb, no must also stand before it. The double negative is the correct form, not an error.

units.title: AT HOME
units.subtitle: The rooms of a house, what stands in them, clothing, and animals

tips.b: Hay is one form for both there is and there are. It never changes for number, and it takes un, una, a number or no article at all, never el or la.
Gender is readable beyond -o and -a. Nouns ending in -ción, -sión, -dad and -tad are feminine; nouns ending in -aje, -or and -ma from Greek are masculine.

phrases.t: La llave está en la puerta
phrases.e: The key is in the door
phrases.ipa: la ˈʝa.βe es.ˈta en la ˈpweɾ.ta

tips.b: Este points at what is near the speaker, ese at what is further away. Both agree with the noun: este plato, esta mesa, estos platos, estas mesas.
Possession is built with de, running from the thing owned to the owner. There is no apostrophe form in Spanish, and de plus el contracts to del.

phrases.t: El libro está sobre la mesa
phrases.e: The book is on the table
phrases.ipa: el ˈli.βɾo es.ˈta ˈso.βɾe la ˈme.sa

phrases.t: Hay dos platos en la cocina
phrases.e: There are two plates in the kitchen
phrases.ipa: ˈai dos ˈpla.tos en la ko.ˈsi.na

tips.b: Llevar names both what a person has on and what a person carries along. Usar also serves for wearing a garment or a size.
The colour word stands after the garment and agrees with it in gender and number.

phrases.e: I am wearing a white shirt

phrases.t: Mi abrigo está en la silla
phrases.e: My coat is on the chair
phrases.ipa: mi a.ˈβɾi.ɣo es.ˈta en la ˈsi.ʝa

phrases.e: She is wearing a red dress

tips.b: A double rr between vowels is trilled, and a single r at the start of a word is trilled as well. A single r elsewhere is one short tap. The difference separates two words.
Most animal names carry a fixed gender that says nothing about the animal: la araña and el ratón keep their article for either sex. A few pairs do change, such as el gato and la gata.

phrases.t: Los pájaros están en el árbol
phrases.e: The birds are in the tree
phrases.ipa: los ˈpa.xa.ɾos es.ˈtan en el ˈaɾ.βol

units.title: TIME
units.subtitle: The days, the months, the hours of the day, and the weather

tips.b: Days of the week are written in lower case and take el for a single day and los for a repeated one. No word for on is used.

tips.h: Days ending in -s stay the same
tips.b: Lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves and viernes have one form for singular and plural; only the article changes. Sábado and domingo add -s.
The preterite reports a finished action. In the first person singular an -ar verb ends -é and an -er or -ir verb ends -í.

phrases.e: On Saturday I go to the market

tips.b: Month names are written in lower case and take no article. The preposition en covers in: en enero, en marzo.

tips.h: A date runs day, then month
tips.b: A date is built with the number, de and the month: el doce de octubre. The first of the month is primero, and the other days use plain numbers.

phrases.e: In January it is very cold

phrases.t: Hay doce meses en el año
phrases.e: There are twelve months in the year
phrases.ipa: ˈai ˈdo.se ˈme.ses en el ˈa.ɲo

phrases.t: Vamos a la playa en julio
phrases.e: We go to the beach in July
phrases.ipa: ˈba.mos a la ˈpla.ʝa en ˈxu.ljo

tips.b: The hour is given with son las plus the number, except one o'clock, which takes es la. Minutes are added with y, and a half hour is media.
eg: It is a quarter past seven

tips.b: A named hour takes de la mañana or de la tarde. Without an hour, the general stretch of the day takes por la mañana or por la noche.
eg: a las ocho de la mañana

phrases.t: Son las tres de la tarde
phrases.e: It is three in the afternoon
phrases.ipa: son las ˈtɾes ðe la ˈtaɾ.ðe

phrases.e: I study one hour each day

tips.h: The weather is made, not been
tips.b: Spanish reports most weather with hacer in the third person: hace frío, hace calor, hace sol, hace viento. Está covers cloud and rain in progress.

tips.h: Llover and nevar have no subject
tips.b: Verbs of weather appear only in the third person singular, with nothing standing in front of them. The stem changes: llueve, nieva.

tips.h: Ir a states what comes next
tips.b: A form of ir, then a, then an infinitive announces the near future. It replaces a separate future tense in everyday speech.

phrases.e: It is going to rain tomorrow

units.title: GETTING AROUND
units.subtitle: Places in a town, directions, vehicles, and travel

tips.b: Spanish has two contractions and no others: a and el join as al, de and el join as del. The feminine la never contracts.
Location always takes estar, whatever the building or the country. Ser with a place names an event instead: la fiesta es en el parque.

phrases.e: I go to the market on Saturdays
I work in a big office

tips.b: An instruction to a stranger uses the usted command: an -ar verb ends -e and an -er or -ir verb ends -a. Doblar, seguir and tomar carry most directions.

tips.h: Left and right keep the article
tips.b: Izquierda and derecha are nouns, so they stand with la after a: a la izquierda, a la derecha.

phrases.t: La tienda está a la derecha
phrases.e: The store is on the right
phrases.ipa: la ˈtjen.da es.ˈta a la ðe.ˈɾe.tʃa

tips.b: The means of transport takes en, with no article: en tren, en avión, en bicicleta. Travel on foot is a pie.
Carro is the usual word across most of Latin America, coche is heard in Mexico and Spain, and auto is common in the southern countries. This course uses carro.

phrases.e: I go to work by bus

phrases.t: El tren llega a las ocho
phrases.ipa: el ˈtɾen ˈʝe.ɣa a las ˈo.tʃo

tips.b: Para points forward: a destination, a purpose, a deadline, a recipient. Por looks at cause, duration, exchange and the route taken through a place.

tips.h: Salir and llegar take a preposition
tips.b: Salir de names the place left behind and salir para the place ahead. Llegar a names the place reached.

phrases.t: El avión sale a las nueve
phrases.ipa: el a.ˈβjon ˈsa.le a las ˈnwe.βe

phrases.t: Mi maleta está en el carro
phrases.e: My suitcase is in the car
phrases.ipa: mi ma.ˈle.ta es.ˈta en el ˈka.ro

phrases.t: Regreso el domingo por la tarde
phrases.ipa: re.ˈɣɾe.so el do.ˈmiŋ.ɡo poɾ la ˈtaɾ.ðe

units.title: PEOPLE
units.subtitle: Feelings, the body, health, and how a person looks

tips.b: Gustar means to please, so the thing liked is the subject and the person is an object pronoun in front. One thing takes gusta, several things take gustan.
Estar carries a mood of the moment and ser carries a lasting trait. Está triste reports a bad day; es triste describes a sad person or thing.

tips.h: Tener with a state of the body
tips.b: A set of everyday states is had rather than been: tener hambre, tener sed, tener frío, tener miedo, tener sueño, tener años. Mucho, not muy, strengthens them.
Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, and la mano is the common exception. Nouns ending in -a are usually feminine, against el día, el mapa and el problema.
With doler and with reflexive verbs the body part carries el or la, not a possessive, because the pronoun already names the owner.
The part of the body that hurts is the subject of doler, and the person appears as a pronoun in front: me duele el pie, me duelen los pies.
Illness is a passing condition and takes estar. Ser enfermo would describe a permanent identity and is not used for being unwell.

phrases.e: I have a fever and pain
I sleep eight hours each night

phrases.t: La medicina está en la cocina
phrases.e: The medicine is in the kitchen
phrases.ipa: la me.ði.ˈsi.na es.ˈta en la ko.ˈsi.na

tips.h: Ser for what a person is like
tips.b: A lasting quality of a person takes ser: es alta, es amable, es joven. Estar with the same adjective would report a change or a passing impression.
The ending -ito or -ita shrinks a word or softens its tone. It attaches to nouns, adjectives and a few adverbs, and often carries affection rather than size.

phrases.e: He is a very kind man

phrases.t: El niño rubio es mi hijo
phrases.e: The blond boy is my son
phrases.ipa: el ˈni.ɲo ˈru.βjo es mi ˈi.xo

units.title: WORK AND SCHOOL
units.subtitle: The classroom, jobs, the numbers past twelve, and money

tips.b: When the direct object of a verb is a person, the preposition a stands in front of it. The same verb takes no a before a thing.
The written accent moves or disappears in the plural so that the stressed syllable stays where it was: examen becomes exámenes, lección becomes lecciones. A final z turns into c: lápiz, lápices.

phrases.t: La maestra enseña a los niños
phrases.ipa: la ma.ˈes.tɾa en.ˈse.ɲa a los ˈni.ɲos

phrases.t: Escribo la tarea en el cuaderno
phrases.e: I write the homework in the notebook
phrases.ipa: es.ˈkɾi.βo la ta.ˈɾe.a en el kwa.ˈðeɾ.no

tips.b: After ser a profession stands bare: es maestra, es ingeniero. The article returns as soon as an adjective describes the job.
A job ending in -o changes to -a, and one ending in -or adds -a. Names ending in -e or -ista keep one form and change only the article.

phrases.e: I work at a big company

tips.b: Eleven to fifteen have their own names. Sixteen to nineteen and twenty-one to twenty-nine are written as one word: dieciséis, diecisiete, veintiuno, veintidós.
Above thirty the tens and the units are joined by y and written as three words: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, noventa y nueve.
Cien counts exactly one hundred and stands before a noun. From 101 to 199 the form is ciento, with no y after it.

phrases.t: Hay treinta alumnos en la clase
phrases.e: There are thirty students in the class
phrases.ipa: ˈai ˈtɾein.ta a.ˈlum.nos en la ˈkla.se

phrases.e: The book costs one hundred pesos

tips.b: Costar appears in the third person only, and it agrees with the thing bought: cuesta for one, cuestan for several.

tips.h: Names of money are lower case
tips.b: A currency is an ordinary noun and keeps its article: el peso, el dólar, el euro. The amount comes first and the currency follows.

units.title: OUT AND ABOUT
units.subtitle: Ordering a meal, shopping, pastimes, and sport

tips.b: Quiero states a want plainly. Quisiera softens it to would like and is the ordinary form for ordering food from a stranger.

tips.h: Each meal has its own verb
tips.b: The three meals carry matching verbs: desayunar for breakfast, almorzar for lunch, cenar for dinner. The noun and the verb share a stem.
eg: I have dinner with my family

phrases.e: I would like a coffee with milk

tips.b: Buscar already means to look for, so no preposition follows it. Esperar, mirar and pedir work the same way.
eg: I am looking for a gift
I am waiting for the bus

tips.b: The act of shopping is ir de compras. A single purchase is hacer una compra, and the verb comprar names the buying itself.

phrases.t: Busco un regalo para mi madre
phrases.e: I am looking for a gift for my mother
phrases.ipa: ˈbus.ko un re.ˈɣa.lo ˈpa.ɾa mi ˈma.ðɾe

phrases.e: I buy fruit at the supermarket

tips.h: Two verbs for the word play
tips.b: Jugar covers games and sport and takes a before the name of the game. Tocar covers playing an instrument or any music.
When what pleases is an activity, the infinitive follows gusta and the verb stays singular even with two activities listed.

phrases.e: We are going to a party

phrases.t: Los niños juegan en el parque
phrases.e: The children play in the park
phrases.ipa: los ˈni.ɲos ˈxwe.ɣan en el ˈpaɾ.ke

tips.b: The name of a sport follows jugar with a, which contracts with el to al: jugar al fútbol, jugar al tenis.
Ganar covers both winning a match and earning money, and perder covers both losing a match and losing an object.
eg: He earns a lot of money

phrases.t: Me gusta nadar en el mar
phrases.e: I like swimming in the sea
phrases.ipa: me ˈɡus.ta na.ˈðaɾ en el ˈmaɾ

units.title: THE WORLD
units.subtitle: Landscape, the city, countries and languages, and more verbs

tips.b: H is written and never pronounced: hoja sounds like oja, hola like ola. The only place h is heard is in the pair ch.

tips.h: The article in a general statement
tips.b: A noun taken in general keeps its article, where English drops it: la nieve es blanca, me gustan las montañas.

phrases.t: El río pasa por el bosque
phrases.e: The river runs through the forest
phrases.ipa: el ˈri.o ˈpa.sa poɾ el ˈbos.ke

phrases.t: Las estrellas están en el cielo
phrases.e: The stars are in the sky
phrases.ipa: las es.ˈtɾe.ʝas es.ˈtan en el ˈsje.lo

phrases.t: Veo el sol y la luna
phrases.e: I see the sun and the moon
phrases.ipa: ˈbe.o el ˈsol i la ˈlu.na

tips.h: La gente takes a singular verb
tips.b: Gente is one collective noun, so the verb after it stays singular: la gente habla, la gente camina. English treats people as plural.

tips.h: Por for movement along a place
tips.b: Por marks the route: movement along a street, through a park or around a city. A for the same verb would mark the destination instead.

phrases.t: La gente camina por la calle
phrases.e: The people walk along the street
phrases.ipa: la ˈxen.te ka.ˈmi.na poɾ la ˈka.ʝe

phrases.e: I live in a small town

phrases.t: El edificio está en la plaza
phrases.e: The building is on the square
phrases.ipa: el e.ði.ˈfi.sjo es.ˈta en la ˈpla.sa

phrases.e: There is a lot of noise here

tips.b: A country is capitalised, and the language and the nationality drawn from it are not: España, español; Francia, francés.
Origin is stated with ser and de, and the question is ¿De dónde es? Countries take no article in this pattern.

phrases.e: I am from a small country
I want to travel around the world

tips.b: Querer, poder, pedir and their kind change the vowel of the stem in every form except nosotros: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren.
A verb listed with -se turns its action back on the subject. The pronoun changes with the person and stands before the verb: me llamo, se levanta.
Saber holds facts and skills, and takes an infinitive for an ability. Conocer holds acquaintance with a person, a city or a work, and takes the personal a before a person.

phrases.e: I want to learn another language
